The **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** is a key piece of legislation in the United Kingdom that received Royal Assent on **27 July 2010**. It was introduced by the **Coalition Government** (Conservative-Liberal Democrat) following the **2010 General Election** and implemented several tax changes aimed at reducing the budget deficit, promoting economic stability, and reforming the tax system.

Here’s a detailed breakdown of its key provisions:

---

### **1. Background & Context**
- The **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** was the second Finance Act of 2010 (the first being the **Finance Act 2010**, which was based on the previous Labour Government’s Budget).
- It followed the **June 2010 Emergency Budget** presented by **Chancellor George Osborne**, which outlined austerity measures to tackle the UK’s **£155 billion deficit** (10.2% of GDP at the time).
- The Act introduced **permanent tax changes** (unlike temporary measures in the first Finance Act 2010) and set the stage for long-term fiscal consolidation.

---

### **2. Key Provisions of the Act**
#### **A. Income Tax & National Insurance**
1. **Personal Allowance Increase**
   - The **income tax personal allowance** (tax-free threshold) was increased by **£1,000** to **£7,475** for 2011-12 (from £6,475 in 2010-11), benefiting basic-rate taxpayers.
   - This was part of a **long-term plan** to raise the allowance to **£10,000** (later achieved in 2014-15).

2. **Higher-Rate Tax Threshold Freeze**
   - The **40% income tax threshold** was **frozen** at **£43,875** (from £43,875 in 2010-11), meaning more people would be dragged into the higher tax band due to wage inflation (**fiscal drag**).

3. **National Insurance Contributions (NICs) Changes**
   - The **upper earnings limit** for NICs was **aligned with the higher-rate tax threshold** (£43,875), reducing the anomaly where high earners paid NICs on a lower income cap.
   - **Employer NICs threshold** was increased by **£21 per week** to reduce the burden on small businesses.

4. **Pension Tax Relief Restrictions**
   - The **annual allowance** for pension contributions was **reduced from £255,000 to £50,000** (effective April 2011).
   - The **lifetime allowance** was **cut from £1.8m to £1.5m** (later reduced further in subsequent budgets).
   - High earners (income > £150,000) saw **tax relief tapered**, reducing the incentive for wealthy individuals to use pensions for tax planning.

---

#### **B. Corporation Tax & Business Taxes**
1. **Corporation Tax Rate Cuts**
   - The **main rate of corporation tax** was **reduced from 28% to 27%** (effective April 2011), with further cuts planned to **24% by 2014**.
   - The **small profits rate** (for companies with profits < £300,000) was **cut from 21% to 20%**.

2. **Bank Levy Introduction**
   - A **new Bank Levy** was introduced, charging **0.075%** on the **balance sheets of UK banks and building societies** (later increased to **0.105%** in 2011).
   - Aimed at **recovering costs of the financial crisis** and discouraging excessive risk-taking.

3. **Capital Allowances Changes**
   - The **annual investment allowance (AIA)** was **increased from £50,000 to £100,000** (temporarily) to encourage business investment.
   - **Writing-down allowances** for plant and machinery were **reduced from 20% to 18%** (main rate) and **10% to 8%** (special rate).

4. **Controlled Foreign Companies (CFC) Rules Reform**
   - The Act **tightened CFC rules** to prevent multinational companies from shifting profits offshore to avoid UK tax.
   - Later reforms (in **Finance Act 2012**) introduced a **territorial tax system** to make the UK more competitive.

---

#### **C. Value-Added Tax (VAT)**
1. **VAT Rate Increase**
   - The **standard VAT rate was increased from 17.5% to 20%** (effective **4 January 2011**).
   - This was a **major revenue-raising measure**, expected to generate **£13 billion per year**.
   - Some **exemptions remained** (e.g., food, children’s clothes, books), but many goods and services became more expensive.

2. **VAT Registration Threshold**
   - The **VAT registration threshold** was **increased from £70,000 to £73,000** (later adjusted for inflation).

---

#### **D. Capital Gains Tax (CGT) Reforms**
1. **CGT Rate Increase for Higher Earners**
   - The **CGT rate for higher-rate taxpayers** was **increased from 18% to 28%** (effective **23 June 2010**).
   - **Basic-rate taxpayers** continued to pay **18%** (later **10%** in 2016).
   - **Entrepreneurs’ Relief** was **retained at 10%** (with a **lifetime limit of £5m**).

2. **Indexation Allowance Freeze**
   - The **indexation allowance** (which adjusted gains for inflation) was **frozen** for individuals and trusts (later abolished in 2018).

---

#### **E. Inheritance Tax (IHT) & Stamp Duty**
1. **IHT Threshold Freeze**
   - The **nil-rate band (threshold) for IHT** was **frozen at £325,000** until **2014-15** (later extended to **2020-21**).
   - This meant more estates would be liable for IHT due to rising property prices.

2. **Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) Changes**
   - **First-time buyer relief** was **extended** (temporarily) for properties up to **£250,000** (0% SDLT).
   - **Higher-rate SDLT (5%)** was introduced for **residential properties over £1m** (effective April 2011).

---

#### **F. Anti-Avoidance & Compliance Measures**
1. **Disclosure of Tax Avoidance Schemes (DOTAS) Expansion**
   - The Act **extended DOTAS** to cover more tax avoidance schemes, requiring promoters to disclose them to HMRC.

2. **General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR) Precursor**
   - While the **GAAR was later introduced in 2013**, this Act **strengthened anti-avoidance powers**, including:
     - **Accelerated payment notices** (for disputed tax).
     - **Follower notices** (forcing taxpayers to amend returns if a similar scheme was defeated in court).

3. **Offshore Tax Evasion Crackdown**
   - **New penalties** for offshore tax evasion, including **higher fines (up to 200% of tax owed)** for non-compliance.
   - **New disclosure facilities** for offshore account holders to regularise their affairs.

---

#### **G. Other Measures**
1. **Fuel Duty Increase**
   - **Fuel duty was increased by 1p per litre** (October 2010), with further **annual increases planned** (later modified due to public pressure).

2. **Alcohol & Tobacco Duties**
   - **Beer duty increased by 2% above inflation**.
   - **Cider duty increased by 10% above inflation** (later reversed after backlash).
   - **Tobacco duty increased by 2% above inflation**.

3. **Child Trust Fund (CTF) Abolition**
   - The **CTF was scrapped** for new applicants (replaced by the **Junior ISA** in 2011).

4. **Tax Credits & Welfare Changes**
   - **Child Tax Credit** was **reduced for higher earners** (income > £40,000).
   - **Working Tax Credit** eligibility was **tightened**.

---

### **3. Economic & Political Impact**
#### **A. Fiscal Consolidation**
- The Act was a **cornerstone of the UK’s austerity programme**, aiming to **reduce the deficit by £40 billion by 2014-15**.
- The **VAT increase** was particularly controversial, as it **disproportionately affected lower-income households** (VAT is regressive).

#### **B. Business & Investment Response**
- **Corporation tax cuts** were welcomed by businesses, improving the UK’s **competitiveness** (later leading to a **19% rate by 2017**).
- The **bank levy** was criticised by financial institutions but seen as necessary to **recover bailout costs**.
- **Pension tax relief changes** led to **reduced contributions from high earners**.

#### **C. Public & Political Reaction**
- **Labour opposed the VAT increase**, arguing it would harm economic recovery.
- **Liberal Democrats** (coalition partners) **compromised on VAT** in exchange for **income tax threshold increases**.
- **Small businesses benefited** from NICs relief and higher AIA, but **consumers faced higher costs** due to VAT and fuel duty.

---

### **4. Later Amendments & Legacy**
- Many provisions were **further adjusted in later Finance Acts** (e.g., **Finance Act 2011, 2012, 2013**).
- The **VAT rate remains at 20%** (as of 2024).
- The **personal allowance eventually reached £12,570** (2023-24).
- The **bank levy was later modified** (e.g., **8% surcharge on bank profits** introduced in 2016).
- The **CGT rate for residential property was increased to 28%** (2023).

---
### **5. Key Takeaways**
| **Measure** | **Change** | **Impact** |
|-------------|-----------|------------|
| **Income Tax** | Personal allowance ↑ to £7,475 | More low earners tax-free |
| **Higher Rate Threshold** | Frozen at £43,875 | Fiscal drag → more taxpayers at 40% |
| **VAT** | ↑ from 17.5% to 20% | £13bn/year revenue, but regressive |
| **Corporation Tax** | Main rate ↓ to 27% | Business-friendly, later cut to 19% |
| **Bank Levy** | 0.075% on liabilities | £2.5bn/year from banks |
| **CGT** | Higher rate ↑ to 28% | Reduced tax avoidance via capital gains |
| **Pensions** | Annual allowance ↓ to £50k | Less tax relief for high earners |
| **Anti-Avoidance** | Stricter DOTAS & penalties | Crackdown on tax evasion |

---
### **6. Where to Find the Full Text?**
- **Official Legislation**: [Finance (No. 2) Act 2010 (UK Parliament)](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/38/contents)
- **Explanatory Notes**: [HMRC Guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/finance-no-2-act-2010)
- **Budget 2010 Documents**: [HM Treasury Archive](https://www.gov.uk/government/collections/budget-2010)

---
### **7. Conclusion**
The **Finance (No. 2) Act 2010** was a **landmark austerity budget** that:
✅ **Raised revenues** (VAT, CGT, bank levy).
✅ **Cut business taxes** (corporation tax, capital allowances).
✅ **Tightened anti-avoidance rules**.
✅ **Shifted the tax burden** slightly from income to consumption.

It set the tone for **UK fiscal policy in the 2010s**, balancing **deficit reduction** with **economic growth incentives**. Many of its measures remain in place today, though some (like the **VAT rate**) have become permanent fixtures of the UK tax system.
